Article Title: “I wouldn’t, probably help you": President Donald Trump tells 10-year-old rescued by teen lifeguard he “wouldn’t” have risked his life to save him
Article Text:
The heroic rescue

Lifeguards as first responders ?

Ryder’s rescue of Nathanial unfolded as California state lawmakers reviewed proposed legislation that would officially make lifeguards first responders.

Nathanial Rai had been swept off his feet along the California coast and was rescued by a 16-year-old lifeguard, Ryder Williams. The video of the brave rescue went viral across social media, enough to be noticed by the United States President Donald Trump . On Monday, August 17, he invited both Rai and Williams to the White House for a meeting.While the gesture was appreciated what made many more headlines was the statement made by the 80-year-old world leader. Of Williams, Trump said to Rai: “He’s a real hero. I don’t know if I’d do it. I wouldn’t, probably. You’re lucky I wasn’t on the service that day.”Rai, 10, donned a dark suit and maroon tie and sat on a gold couch beside his father and Trump. Across from him was Ryder and both watched Trump speak of their ordeal, a video of which went viral on the internet. The President met the lifeguard and Nathanial after saying the teen deserved a civilian honour. Trump previously said on social media that he also would be inviting Ryder to the White House to reward his bravery.During the conversation, Williams was asked about his thought process during the heroic rescue. “In those dangerous moments that we have, we fall back on our training, and we are trained so well by many to handle that situation as best we can,” he said.“I was really thinking about getting the boy out of the water as fast as I can.”He added that he wants to continue helping people and hoped to go to paramedic school and become a firefighter. “I hope everyone can take away from this is to help more people,” Williams said. “Try to look out for everyone around you, and just try to help everybody out as much as you can.”A dramatic video of the rescue went viral in late July. It showed Ryder clinging to Nathaniel as pounding waves repeatedly crashed over them. The pair disappeared from view and reemerged after several seconds as the wave receded. A second lifeguard, Aaron Bohnen, was eventually able to help get them both back to shore at Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz, California.Trump initially commented on the video in response to a post from his son, Eric Trump, who said Ryder deserved “the highest civilian honour”. Meanwhile, Nathanial’s father, Sumit, told the Associated Press of Ryder: “What he did, I can never repay. I’m forever grateful.”Williams previously detailed the rescue in a video and statement for the official California State Parks Instagram account. He said he was standing at the waterline near Seabright's Tower 2 when he "saw a child about 20 yards up from the tower lose his footing in ankle-deep water," he recalled. “I radioed it in, threw my radio and sunglasses at the base of my tower as I ran toward the kid,” he wrote in the post’s caption. “I put my fins on my wrist, popped my buoy and entered the water to get a hold of the child. ”The teen said he couldn’t get a tube to the boy and wasn’t able to pull him out of the rough waves “because he was limp and the waves were pushing so hard.” “As I grab the child, he goes limp, so I’m thinking about if he’s unconscious or not, that I really need to go in,” Williams recalled in the clip. “The whole time I was thinking, ‘I just need to hold my position until my partner can get here because I’m not going to be able to get him out on my own. ’ ”“My partner mostly takes over holding the child because at this point, my arms were very exhausted from holding on,” Williams recalled. “I still support him as much as I can as we drag him out of the water.” The teen said that he and Bohnen got Rai safely back to shore and used a medical kit to help treat his injuries. Soon after, Williams was back to work “making more rescues later that day.”After the incident, Rai told CBS Mornings on August 4, that he thought he “was going to die” before Williams came in the water. He explained that he had never experienced waves that powerful before — and had seen surf that large “only on, like, the internet.”As NBC Bay Area reported, Ryder’s rescue of Nathanial unfolded as California state lawmakers reviewed proposed legislation that would officially make lifeguards first responders. The outlet noted that analysts say giving lifeguards first responder status would bring them more professional recognition, support and resources, and could offer them better worker protections and benefits. It also spoke with people who could not believe that lifeguards were not already first responders.However, as per John Laird, a Santa Cruz state senator, such a designation is not straightforward. “Of course, lifeguards are first responders, but first responders also go through this rigorous training, so you’d have to decide – because in the peace officer standards training you go through eight months of training – so you’d have to decide what’s appropriate here,” NBC Bay Area quoted Laird as saying.“How does it work? How does it get designated? What training comes with it? Who pays for it?”
Article Summary: Ryder Williams, 16, rescued Nathanial Rai, 10, from the water at Seabright State Beach in Santa Cruz, California. Video of the rescue went viral across social media, enough to be noticed by the United States President Donald Trump. On Monday, August 17, he invited both Rai and Williams to the White House for a meeting.

Article Title: Tropical Storm Lala in Hawaii: Roads collapse, 100 homes swept away, no power, mobile service; 1 dead
Article Text:
Tropical Storm Lala strengthened on the Big Island of Hawaii (Picture credit: AP)

Southern Big Island communities remain cut off

Cleanup begins as outages persist

Lala moves west, surf and landslide risks remain

Hawaii officials linked one death on Monday to Tropical Storm Lala after a woman reported missing from Naalehu on the Big Island was found dead. Authorities did not immediately release further information about her or how she died.The death was confirmed a day after Governor Josh Green said no one was believed to have died when about 100 homes were swept from their foundations and washed away on the Big Island. Authorities have since said no one is believed to be missing following the destruction.Lala had been a hurricane while approaching Hawaii but weakened to tropical-storm strength on Sunday as it moved past the islands without making landfall. Heavy rain and winds brought down trees from downtown Honolulu to the Big Island and triggered flash floods.The storm continued moving west away from Hawaii and was expected to regain hurricane strength over open water, far from land, by Wednesday.Collapsed roads, debris and communication failures continued to isolate several communities in the hard-hit southern end of the Big Island as officials assessed the damage.Jeanné Kapela, a state representative whose Kau district includes some of the affected areas, said the district was "in shambles".Punaluu, a community of about 100 households known for its black-sand beach, was among the places cut off, the Associated Press reported.With power and mobile phone service unavailable in some areas, Kapela was trying to arrange satellite internet connections for residents.Kapela said the damage had hit a rural part of Hawaii that receives far less attention than tourist destinations such as Lahaina and Waikiki. She noted that the area includes the southernmost point in the United States."That's the community that got hit. And it's probably one of the most rural communities in the entire country," she said.Green said he expected access to the affected communities to be restored within days rather than weeks.Flooding also damaged burial grounds in Naalehu. Kapela said two cemeteries had been "washed out".Green asked people to respect the affected burial sites after floodwaters displaced iwi kupuna, the Hawaiian term for sacred ancestral skeletal remains of Native Hawaiians.Tom Callis, an official with Hawaii County, said the affected cemetery areas had been cordoned off and no work was taking place there.Crews repaired bridges and cleared fallen trees on Monday, while motorists were urged to use alternative routes.Public schools across Hawaii, along with some private schools and state offices, remained closed on Monday. Schools and county offices on the Big Island were to stay closed on Tuesday.More than 117,000 Hawaiian Electric customers remained without power after winds brought down trees, utility poles and transmission towers. The utility described damage to the Big Island's power transmission system as "extensive".Emergency communications were also disrupted. The 911 emergency number on the Big Island temporarily went out of service after the storm affected radio and telephone communications, the Hawaii Police Department said. Service was restored by Monday afternoon, though some disruptions persisted.Green said the recovery would be "somewhat brisk". "And in spite of this loss of one beautiful person," he said, referring to the storm-related death, "it could have been a lot worse."Laupahoehoe, on the northeast coast of the Big Island, recorded about 1.1 metres of rain, the highest measured total from the storm.The strongest gusts were recorded atop Mauna Kea at 225kmph. At lower elevations across the island chain, winds reached 48-64kmph, with gusts of up to 97kmph, National Weather Service meteorologist Patrick Blood said.Hawaii had no coastal watches or warnings in effect on Monday, according to the National Hurricane Center, but dangerous surf and rip currents remained.People were also advised to avoid brown or murky coastal waters.The heavy rain left the ground saturated, keeping the risk of landslides in some areas, although winds were no longer considered a threat."There's no real looming hazards that we're facing now," Blood said. "Lala's off to the west."Federal officials have pledged recovery help. US Senator Brian Schatz said he had discussed federal support with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and urged approval of an expected emergency funding request for debris clearance and repairs to damaged roads and highways.
Article Summary: Woman reported missing from Naalehu on the Big Island found dead. Death confirmed a day after Governor Josh Green said no one was believed to have died when about 100 homes were swept from their foundations and washed away. Lala had been a hurricane while approaching Hawaii but weakened to tropical-storm strength.

Article Title: 'What you did was incredible': Trump meets California's teenage lifeguard and the boy he rescued
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump speaks as he meets with lifeguard Ryder Williams, left, in the Oval Office of the White House, in Washington, as Nathaniel Rai and Shane Williams listen. (AP)

(With AP inputs)

US President Donald Trump on Monday (local time) met a teenage lifeguard and the boy he rescued off the California coast, praising the rescue and the boy’s composure during the ordeal as “incredible.”Sixteen-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams and 10-year-old Nathaniel Rai were honoured at a White House ceremony also attended by their families, days after Trump announced that he would invite the pair to recognise their bravery.“What you did was incredible, and everybody saw it,” he told the duo, referring to a viral video of the July rescue in Santa Cruz. “When I first saw it, I said, ‘roll that back, I want to see that again.’”Asked about the moment, Williams credited his training for helping him react quickly.“In those dangerous moments that we have, we always try to fall back on our training,” he recalled. “I really was thinking about how to get the boy out of the water as fast as I can.”Nathaniel, seated beside his father and sister, nodded as Trump recounted the rescue.“Your father is the happiest man in the world,” the president told him, adding that the boy deserved respect for how he handled the emergency.“The way Nathaniel handled it was — he was cool, considering the problems.”Trump then invited the pair to see the Lincoln Bedroom at the White House. When Williams spoke about his ambition to become a firefighter, the president suggested he might be getting “some good recommendations.”“He’s a real hero,” Trump added. “I don’t know if I’d do it. I wouldn’t probably. You’re lucky I wasn’t on the service that day.”After the rescue video drew widespread attention online last month, Trump joined others in sharing the footage. In a post on Truth Social, he called for the boys to be honoured.During the Oval Office ceremony, he also praised Williams for his “tremendous grace” during the rescue.“It’s so amazing to see this happen, to see it before your eyes,” Trump remarked. “I’ve seen rescues before. I’ve never seen anything quite like this.”Videos of the rescue have been viewed millions of times worldwide. The footage shows Williams holding onto Nathaniel as powerful waves repeatedly crash over them. At one point, the two disappear underwater for several seconds before emerging from the surf, with Williams continuing to pull Nathaniel toward shore.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump met a teenage lifeguard and the boy he rescued off the California coast. Ryder Williams and 10-year-old Nathaniel Rai were honoured at a White House ceremony also attended by their families. Trump invited the pair to see the Lincoln Bedroom at the White House.

Article Title: US Supreme Court again rejects Donald Trump's bid to overturn $5 million E Jean Carroll verdict
Article Text:
File photo: US President Donald Trump and writer E Jean Carroll

Jury found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation

Separate $83.3 million Carroll case still before Supreme Court

The US Supreme Court on Monday again rejected President Donald Trump 's attempt to overturn a $5 million civil verdict in favour of writer E Jean Carroll, leaving in place a jury's finding that he sexually abused and defamed her.The justices declined Trump's request to reconsider their decision in June not to hear his appeal of the 2023 verdict.The court's order was unsigned and gave no explanation. The Supreme Court rarely agrees to rehear cases it has already declined to take up.Trump's lawyers had argued that the trial was unfair and that the court should reconsider its earlier decision.The case stems from Carroll's allegation that Trump sexually assaulted her in a dressing room at the Bergdorf Goodman department store in Manhattan in the mid-1990s.Carroll, a former advice columnist for Elle magazine, first publicly accused Trump of raping her in 2019. Trump denied the allegation and repeatedly accused her of lying.The case that resulted in the $5 million verdict focused on Trump's statements in 2022, when he described Carroll's allegation as a “hoax” and a “con job” on social media.A jury in 2023 found Trump liable for sexually abusing Carroll and defaming her, but it did not find him liable for rape, as Carroll had alleged.Trump paid nearly $5.63 million following the Supreme Court's decision in June, with the amount including the original $5 million judgment and interest, according to Reuters.Carroll's lawyer, Roberta Kaplan, welcomed Monday's decision.“We are pleased that the United States Supreme Court has declined again to hear this case,” Kaplan said.“As a result, the jury's unanimous verdict that Donald Trump sexually assaulted and then defamed E. Jean Carroll is now final and cannot be challenged in any court,” she added.Trump still has another appeal before the Supreme Court involving Carroll. That case concerns a separate $83.3 million jury verdict over statements he made about her in 2019, while he was president.Trump and the Justice Department argue that presidential immunity protects him from Carroll's defamation lawsuit over those statements. The Supreme Court has not yet decided whether to hear that appeal.The two Carroll cases are civil lawsuits and are separate from the Supreme Court's landmark 2024 ruling on presidential immunity in criminal cases. In that ruling, the court held that former presidents have absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for actions within their core constitutional powers.Trump has consistently denied Carroll's allegations and has maintained that the legal proceedings against him were unfair.
Article Summary: Jury in 2023 found Trump liable for sexually abusing Carroll and defaming her. But it did not find him liable for rape, as Carroll had alleged. Trump still has another appeal before the Supreme Court involving Carroll. That case concerns a separate $83.3 million jury verdict.

Article Title: ‘Has always treated me with great respect’: Trump’s fresh praise for Kim Jong Un
Article Text:
Donald Trump has praised Kim Jong Un once again

(With ANI inputs)

US President Donald Trump said on Monday (local time) that Kim Jong Un has “always treated me with great respect" after citing his "very good" relationship with the North Korean leader to “ substantially reduce ” joint military exercises with South Korea“Kim Jong Un has always treated me with great respect. We met on two main occasions, spoke and spent time together. I understand him, and he understands me. I get along with him,” he told reporters, referring to their meetings during his first term.Trump also contrasted his relationship with Kim with the North Korean leader’s reported views of previous US presidents.“He (Kim) didn’t like Biden, he didn’t like Obama, he didn’t like anybody, but I get along with him very well. What I’m doing now is making things safer — just the opposite,” the Republican added.Earlier, in a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump expressed his dissatisfaction with the United States’ previous agreement to participate in joint military exercises with South Korea.“Based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea, I am not happy with the fact that the United States has, long ago, agreed to participate in Joint Military Exercises with South Korea,” he wrote.The US president characterised the exercises as costly and argued that they send a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea, which he claimed has remained “unthreatening and respectful” during his presidency.While acknowledging that it was "too late" to cancel the exercises altogether, Trump instructed Hegseth to substantially scale them back.On August 15, Trump shared a throwback photograph with Kim, joking that despite their “unfriendly look” in the picture, the two leaders “get along GREAT.”“Despite the unfriendly look on this particular picture, there are many where we’re smiling. Kim Jong Un and I get along GREAT!” he wrote.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Kim Jong Un has “always treated me with great respect” Trump cited his “very good’ relationship with the North Korean leader to “ substantially reduce ” joint military exercises with South Korea.

Article Title: Meta goes to trial this week, which, if it loses, could change Insta & FB forever
Article Text:
Meta

Of the thousands of lawsuits Meta faces over child safety on its platforms, none may be more consequential than one going to trial this week in California. States are seeking extensive financial damages that could, in theory, total as much as $1.4 trillion, plus changes to how the company operates Facebook and Instagram.The lawsuit accuses the social media giant of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by knowingly and deliberately designing features that get children addicted to its platforms. It also claims that Meta routinely collects data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent, in violation of federal law. “Meta has harnessed powerful and unprecedented technologies to entice, engage, and ultimately ensnare youth and teens. Its motive is profit, and in seeking to maximise its financial gains,” the lawsuit says.Dozens of states filed the lawsuit three years ago. The trial, which is set to begin Tuesday in federal court in California, features four of the states as plaintiffs — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey. The other 25 states are expected to have trials later.Meta said it disputes the allegations, and the trial evidence will show its commitment to supporting young people.“We’ve listened to parents, worked with experts and law enforcement, and conducted in-depth research to understand the issues that matter most,” the company said in a statement.For Meta, which already lost two pivotal legal cases over harms to children and teens this year, the stakes are high. The company reported a rare profit decline last month, in part due to $2.4 billion in legal expenses.The $1.4 trillion figure, which Meta disclosed in a legal filing, is almost as high as the Menlo Park, California, company’s entire market capitalisation — that is, the value of all its outstanding shares on the stock market. Paying it would inevitably put Meta Platforms in bankruptcy and perhaps put the company under state ownership.Meta calls the possible penalty “untethered to any claimed violation” by the states. “A sanction of that size has no an­alogue in the history of consumer protection enforcement,” Meta said in a July 6 filing with the US district court for the no­rthern district of California.If Meta loses the trial, the court would have wide discretion over the size of any financial penalty, and legal experts say anything close to $1.4 trillion would be unlikely. “It’s not plausible in the sense that Meta doesn’t have that much money and could not get it,” said James Grimmelmann, a law professor at Cornell Law School and Cornell Tech. “An award that large would put Meta into bankruptcy, wipe out its owners, and effectively result in the states owning Meta. ”As a practical matter, Grimmelmann added, “that seems extremely unlikely to happen.”In other cases that have involved high potential damages for multiple individual offences, he said courts have stopped short of imposing the maximum penalties. One example is the Anthropic artificial intelligence training case, where plaintiffs were claiming damages of $150,000 per book that Anthropic copied, but the penalty ended up being $3,000 per book, totalling about $1.5 billion.
Article Summary: Dozens of states filed the lawsuit three years ago. The trial, which is set to begin Tuesday in federal court in California, features four of the states as plaintiffs. Paying it would inevitably put Meta Platforms in bankruptcy and perhaps put the company under state ownership.

Article Title: Fake Iran nuclear post: How a fabricated X claim by Indian account created panic in Israel, US
Article Text:
Donald Trump, Mojtaba Khamenei, Benjamin Netanyahu

False quote gains traction in Israel

False claim reaches Washington

How the narrative gained credibility

What Iran has said about its nuclear programme

A fabricated quote attributed to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards commander spread from an Indian X account to Israeli media and US politicians, eventually featuring in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech, according to a review by The New York Times.The false claim emerged on August 5, when an anonymous account on X in India posted that Brig. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi had said Iran would not abandon its nuclear weapons ambitions as long as Israel and the United States possessed such weapons.There is no evidence that Vahidi made the statement, or that Iran has developed nuclear weapons. Yet the claim quickly gained traction, with Israeli accounts and media outlets repeating it before it reached senior political figures in Israel and the United States.The episode, detailed by The New York Times, shows how an unverified social media post can acquire credibility as it is repeatedly cited by politicians, broadcasters and other accounts, even when its original source is unreliable.The fabricated quotation was first known to have appeared on an Indian X account with around 175,000 followers. The account has previously faced criticism from fact-checkers and Pakistan's government for allegedly spreading false and Islamophobic content, according to The New York Times.The post included a photograph of Vahidi alongside a cartoonish, AI-generated mushroom cloud. The English text also contained spelling and grammatical errors.Around two hours later, another Indian account with about 82,000 followers shared the same claim in Hindi. According to the Israeli fact-checking organisation Bodkim Project, that account had published another fabricated quote attributed to Vahidi a week earlier.The narrative gained wider attention after it was shared by Mossad Commentary, a prominent Israeli X account that has no known connection to Israel's Mossad intelligence agency.“The regime is not preparing to abandon its nuclear ambitions. It is buying time. There will be no deal,” the account posted.The account is run by Gedaliah Blum, an entrepreneur who leads the Heartland Institute, which organises tours and promotional exchanges in Israel.Blum told The New York Times that he believed the quotation came from a radio interview with Vahidi, although he could not remember the source. He said he shared it because he believed Iran was determined to acquire a nuclear weapon, despite uncertainty over “whether those exact words were spoken.”About 30 minutes later, Israel's Channel 14 shared the quotation in English and claimed it represented the first public acknowledgement by Iran that it was pursuing a nuclear bomb. The post was viewed more than 440,000 times, according to The New York Times.The claim then reached Yair Netanyahu, the son of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Within hours, it appeared in the prime minister's speech at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem.“We heard today the commander of the I.R.G.C., Vahidi, explicitly declaring Iran’s intention to keep developing nuclear weapons,” Netanyahu said.A spokesman for Netanyahu did not explain how the fabricated quotation came to be included in the speech, according to The New York Times, but defended the prime minister's longstanding warnings about Iran's nuclear programme.On Azriel, a co-founder of the Bodkim fact-checking organisation, said the quotation “gained credibility every time an outlet or a politician repeated it,” helping drive its spread.The claim soon crossed into the United States, where it was amplified by senior political figures and Fox News.Mike Waltz, the Trump administration's ambassador to the United Nations, reposted the quotation and wrote that Iran was “finally admitting what’s been obvious for years”.Republican Senator Rick Scott of Florida also shared the claim on social media.Fox News host Bill Hemmer cited the purported statement during an interview with retired US Central Command commander Gen. Joseph L. Votel.“That’s as close to an admission as I have heard, and we’ve been watching this story for years,” Hemmer said.The narrative subsequently began to unravel. Waltz's post was removed from X, although no explanation was given. Neither Waltz nor the White House responded to requests for comment from The New York Times.Fox News later acknowledged the problem. On Thursday, after inquiries from The New York Times, Hemmer read a statement on air saying Fox had learned that the quote was “unverified and inaccurate.”Scott's post remained online, as did the original posts containing the fabricated quotation and thousands of responses treating it as genuine. Scott did not respond to a request for comment from The New York Times.Experts described the episode as an example of “narrative laundering”, in which an unverified or false claim is repeatedly passed between accounts and institutions until it appears to have multiple independent sources.“This quote was clearly crafted to drive a wedge into peace negotiations,” said Darren L. Linvill of Clemson University's Media Forensics Hub, who tracks the spread of disinformation and propaganda on social media.“It is a simple campaign,” he added, “but simple campaigns can still be very effective, and this seems to have certainly had bang for the buck.”The sequence also illustrates how the apparent credibility of a claim can increase as it moves from social media accounts to television networks and political speeches, despite no new evidence being introduced.The New York Times found it unclear who fabricated the quotation. However, the claim appeared to reinforce an existing narrative promoted by Netanyahu that Iran was determined to develop nuclear weapons and that military action against Tehran was necessary.Iran's nuclear programme has remained a major source of international concern and diplomatic negotiations for decades. Tehran has maintained that its nuclear activities have civilian purposes rather than a military objective, although the precise status of its nuclear development remains contested.Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei criticised the fabricated claim and described it as “an example of the flood of lies against the Islamic republic.”He blamed Israel for the narrative but did not provide evidence to support the allegation.“The allegations of a link to a nuclear bomb are based on the same thing, a lie they have been feeding the international community for 20 years to justify military aggression,” he told reporters on Sunday.Vahidi, who took command of the Revolutionary Guards in March, has issued numerous statements during the conflict but has not made the purported declaration about developing nuclear weapons.Last year, after a 12-day conflict with Israel that ended with US airstrikes, Vahidi discussed Iran's nuclear position in an interview with state media. He said Iran would “do things it has not done previously” to defend itself, while adding that the country's position on nuclear weapons “has been stated with complete clarity in the past.”The false quotation therefore did not represent a new declaration by Iran's military leadership, despite being presented that way by several accounts and media outlets.The episode has underscored the risks of relying on viral social media claims during periods of heightened tensions, particularly when those claims concern nuclear weapons, military action and ongoing peace negotiations.
Article Summary: fabricated quote attributed to Iran's Revolutionary Guards commander spread from an Indian X account to Israeli media and US politicians. There is no evidence that Vahidi made the statement, or that Iran has developed nuclear weapons. The episode shows how an unverified social media post can acquire credibility as it is repeatedly cited by politicians, broadcasters and other accounts.

Article Title: Europe wildfires: 2 dead, 500 evacuated as twin blazes hit Greek island near Athens
Article Text:
Two people have died in fires that broke out simultaneously Sunday on the island of Salamis near Athens, the local fire department said. (Photo: @CGTNOfficial)

200 firefighters try to keep Salamina fires apart

Belgium fire burns 30 sq km in High Fens

Less snow and Arctic ice expose darker surfaces that absorb more sunlight, while dry soils and persistent high pressure allow more heat to build over land.

European countries send aircraft, helicopters

France evacuates 650 as fires spread across region

UK battles 14 wildfires as blazes hit Germany, Croatia

Paris touched 40.9°C and Madrid 39.5°C in 2026, while Brussels, London and Bern all recorded highs of 35°C or more.

Europe warmed by about 0.5°C per decade over 1991–2021, against a recent global rate of 0.2°C. Part of the gap reflects geography: Europe’s figure is largely land-based, while the global measure includes oceans.

Two wildfires that broke out minutes apart on the Greek island of Salamina on Sunday killed two people and prompted the evacuation of about 500 people by sea, as crews raced to prevent the fires from joining.The emergency began at 2.40pm local time in Peristeria in the island's south, where strong winds pushed flames through a wooded residential area. About 20 minutes later, another fire was reported in the eastern town of Selinia. Officials had not established the cause of either blaze.About 37,000 people live on Salamina, west of Athens, and many of them are elderly. Authorities had placed the island at high wildfire risk on Sunday as winds approached gale force.“These conditions enabled the fire to quickly reach dangerous proportions and spread rapidly within seven minutes toward nearby residential areas,” fire brigadier general Vasileios Vathrakogiannis said, news agency AP reported.Fire crews found two bodies in Peristeria.The local mayor told Greek media that the dead were believed to be a couple. Greek health minister Adonis Georgiades said on X that at least 10 others had burns or showed “symptoms of smoke inhalation”.Five were taken for treatment locally.Firefighters were deployed across Salamina, backed by 50 fire engines, aircraft, water tankers and construction machinery. Deputy mayor Thodoris Zannis said crews were trying to stop the fires from spreading over a mountain and joining to form a single blaze.About 500 people, including beachgoers, were evacuated by sea. Firefighting and coast guard vessels joined the operation, while five patrol boats and several private vessels were also sent to assist.One of the fires was under control and the evacuation operation had ended by Sunday evening, according to Greek media. Crews were still dealing with scattered fires around Peristeria late on Sunday, while officials said the Selinia blaze had “no active front”.Two coast guard vessels and a fire department vessel were to stay in the area to provide assistance and keep watch.The fires on Salamina were part of a wider outbreak across Europe over the weekend, with crews also battling major blazes in Belgium, France, the UK, Germany and Croatia.By Sunday, the fire in eastern Belgium's High Fens, or Hautes Fagnes, had burned about 30 sq km, making it one of the country's worst wildfires in recent history. Crews were on their third day of operations in Belgium's largest nature reserve, where the affected area had more than doubled within 24 hours, BBC reported.The 30 sq km burned was already more than twice the nearly 14 sq km lost in a 2011 fire in the same area, which had previously been Belgium's largest wildfire on record, according to European Forest Fire Information System data.Shifting winds and spreading smoke prompted authorities on Saturday to order about 600 residents of Waimes and Butgenbach, in Liege province near the German border, to leave their homes. Tourists were advised to leave as well, and a nearby gymnasium was opened to accommodate evacuees.More than 250 emergency personnel were involved in the response, Liege provincial governor Herve Jamar said. They included over 100 firefighters from Belgium and Germany, along with police, military personnel and civil protection staff. Helicopters operated by Belgium's federal police and the Netherlands also supported the operation.Weeks of unusually hot and dry weather had left conditions difficult for crews, with the High Fens' heathland and peat bogs adding to the challenge. Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the Public Service of Wallonia, pointed to the dryness of the ground. “We’re dealing with something much deeper because we have very dry soil,” he said.The fire was still advancing on Sunday in terrain that crews found difficult to reach, according to Rene Dahmen, chief engineer at the Department of Nature and Forest. “On the eastern flank, there’s a line at least a kilometer long where the fire is slowly advancing toward a municipal forest,” Dahmen said. “That’s the first priority now.”Belgian interior minister Bernard Quintin said on X that firefighters had stopped the fire from spreading westwards and towards the German town of Monschau. German authorities said it was about 1.5km from the border on Sunday.Farmers on both sides of the Belgium-Germany border also assisted, using tanker trucks filled with water pumped from a nearby lake before heading towards the fire zone.Belgium had experienced another period of intense heat during the week, with temperatures in parts of the country reaching about 37°C on Friday.Belgium sought international assistance by activating the European Union's civil protection mechanism, EU commissioner for crisis management, with Hadja Lahbib saying “The High Fens are burning. Belgium is not facing it alone,” on X.Sweden provided two water-bombing aircraft. Three helicopters were also being sent — two from the Netherlands and one from the Czech Republic.In southwestern France, about 17 sq km had burned in a pine forest in the Landes region and roughly 650 people had been evacuated. Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul said firefighters encountered no major flare-ups overnight.The Landes fire was the third major blaze in the pine forests of southwestern France this summer, after two others in late July.Elsewhere in the southwest, a fire in neighbouring Gironde department burned about 420 sq km and led authorities to evacuate around 220,000 people as the flames moved towards the Atlantic coast and the Bordeaux area.In the UK, military personnel were supporting emergency crews fighting 14 wildfires in South Wales. More than a dozen homes were gutted by fires in the West Midlands during the week, while temperatures reached 38.1°C on Thursday, the country's hottest day of the year.Firefighters made progress against another blaze in Germany's Hurtgen Forest, allowing about 2,000 residents evacuated from Gey to return on Saturday. By Sunday, officials reported no open flames and said crews had created a cleared cordon around the affected area to stop the fire spreading.Croatia was also dealing with the aftermath of a wildfire along its coastline that began overnight on Friday. At least one person died and dozens were injured, while around 1,200 residents and tourists were evacuated.Croatia's fire chief Slavko Tucakovic called it “one of the worst” blazes in the country's history.The EU's Copernicus climate monitoring service has confirmed that western Europe recorded its hottest June-to-July period on record.Authorities in the UK warned that although the heatwave was easing, drought conditions meant the risk of wildfires remained high.
Article Summary: Two wildfires that broke out minutes apart on the Greek island of Salamina on Sunday killed two people. About 500 people, including beachgoers, were evacuated by sea. Firefighters were deployed across Salamina, backed by 50 fire engines, aircraft, water tankers and construction machinery.

Article Title: Virginia installed 46 water-control structures across 150 miles of old drainage ditches to re-wet a swamp; restored peat now traps 200,000 metric tons of carbon a year
Article Text:
The Fish and Wildlife Service restored peat wetlands at Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge

Restoring water

Volunteers collect native tallgrass prairie seed at Neal Smith National Wildlife Refuge in Iowa.

Water-control structures

Carbon storage

North Carolina’s coastal peatlands are being restored to protect wetlands, reduce wildfire risks and keep carbon stored in the soil. The work is focused on bringing water back to areas that were once drained and altered for farming, timber harvesting and other uses.Peatlands are wetlands whose soils contain large amounts of partly decayed organic matter. They cover only about 3% of the Earth’s surface but store more than twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests, according to The Nature Conservancy. When peat remains wet, it can hold carbon in the soil. But when it dries, it becomes highly flammable and can release large amounts of carbon dioxide when it burns.This makes water management a key part of conservation in coastal North Carolina. Nature-based solutions can improve wildlife habitat while also helping nearby communities through better water quality, recreation and reduced risks from floods and other climate-related threats.One major focus is the Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge in the Albemarle-Pamlico Peninsula. The refuge is one of nine national wildlife refuges in the area, which supports fishing and tourism but faces threats from sea-level rise, storms, flooding and wildfires.With funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, the Fish and Wildlife Service and its partners have restored 37,000 acres of peatland at Pocosin Lakes.At Pocosin Lakes, large areas were once crossed by drainage ditches. Centuries of ditching and draining severely degraded peatlands, while earlier land clearing and drainage also affected the refuge.When peat is kept wet, it is less likely to support intense ground fires. "Restoration is focused on rewetting the peat, stopping artificial drainage and restoring or mimicking the natural movement of water across the refuge," Wendy Stanton, manager of Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge told Public Radio For Eastern North Carolina. She said the restored area now covers more than 37,000 acres.The need for this work became clear during major wildfires. In 2008, lightning started a fire at Pocosin Lakes that burned for three months and destroyed more than 40,000 acres of peat. Meanwhile, the Allen Road fire in 1985 burned through about 100,000 acres, destroyed 26 homes and burned as deeply as three feet into the peat. The fire lasted eight weeks, while an estimated 1 million to 3.8 million metric tons of carbon were released into the air, The Coastal Review reported.Conservation teams are using water-control structures to change how water moves through these drained landscapes. At Pocosin Lakes, the structures can hold back water in drainage systems, helping to restore wetter conditions in the peat. The Nature Conservancy says its teams monitor water levels and adjust the structures to better mimic the natural hydrology of an intact peatland.A similar approach is being used at Angola Bay Game Land. The Nature Conservancy and the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission are working on a restoration design for 7,500 acres of ditched pocosin. Water-control infrastructure began being installed in 2023, with the project also involving plans to restore habitat using wetland species such as Atlantic white cedar, bald cypress, pond cypress and buttonbush.The structures can also be adjusted according to conditions at individual sites. Eric Soderholm, The Nature Conservancy’s coastal wetlands restoration lead in North Carolina, says the approach allows teams to change the effective drainage height by adjusting the boards in the structures. Teams then monitor the results to determine whether water is being held too high or too low.This monitoring is important because the aim is not simply to flood the land. Restoration teams want to create seasonal moisture levels similar to those that would have existed naturally.Keeping peat wet also has implications for climate change. Restored peat wetlands at Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge sequester about 200,000 metric tons of carbon each year. That amount is equivalent to the annual emissions of 42,000 vehicles, according to a US Geological Survey and Fish and Wildlife Service study.It estimates that restoring 10 acres of pocosin peatland is comparable to removing the emissions of 5.3 passenger vehicles per year, while draining 10 acres can have the opposite effect.The restoration programme also involves local communities and landowners because changes to water management can affect farms and other livelihoods. Pocosin Lakes has held meetings with surrounding communities to explain its work and hear concerns. Refuge officials have also worked with farmers on drainage issues.The challenge is becoming more urgent as rising seas and changing weather affect the coastal plain. The Pocosin Lakes water management plan notes that these wetlands may struggle to keep pace if sea levels rise faster than peat can accumulate.
Article Summary: Peatlands are wetlands whose soils contain large amounts of partly decayed organic matter. They store more than twice as much carbon as all the world’s forests. When peat remains wet, it can hold carbon in the soil. But when it dries, it becomes highly flammable and can release large. amounts of carbon dioxide when it burns.

Article Title: Iran offers $30,000 bounty for killing, capturing US soldiers; $60,000 if done by women
Article Text:
Iranian army chief offers $30,000 bounty for killing or capturing US soldiers, doubles reward for women.

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is the best way to reduce tensions between countries? Diplomatic talks Peace agreements 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Iranian Army chief Amir Hatami has announced a $30,000 bounty for anyone who kills or captures a US soldier, with the reward doubled to $60,000 if the act is carried out by an Iranian woman. The announcement comes amid continued tensions between Tehran and Washington, despite there being no known deployment of US ground troops inside Iran.Hatami said the plan was drawn up following "the large number of requests" from people seeking to participate, according to Iran's state-run IRNA news agency. He did not specify where or when any attempt to kill or capture US personnel could take place."Anyone who kills or captures and hands over an invading American military personnel will receive a reward equivalent to $30,000 or 5 billion tomans from the Islamic Republic of Iran's Army," Hatami said, using an informal monetary unit equivalent to 10,000 Iranian rials."Courageous Iranian women who carry out such an action will receive double the reward," he added.The Iranian military chief also reiterated Tehran's demand for the withdrawal of US forces from the region, saying "they no longer have permission to enter the Persian Gulf, the Gulf of Oman or the Strait of Hormuz".Iran's bounty offer amid fragile ceasefireThe announcement comes as the ceasefire between Iran and the US remains fragile, with the two sides continuing to exchange sporadic fire, particularly around southern Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.The conflict began on February 28 after the United States, joined by Israel, launched strikes against Iran. Fighting was followed by an April ceasefire after nearly 40 days of hostilities, while a framework for peace talks reached in June later collapsed.There has been no known deployment of US ground forces inside Iranian territory during the conflict, apart from a rescue mission in April involving US personnel sent to recover the weapons systems officer of a downed F-15.The latest announcement therefore comes without any confirmed US ground presence inside Iran that could be targeted under the bounty.According to the reports, 17 US military personnel have been killed since the conflict began. All of the reported deaths occurred outside Iranian territory, including in Iraq and Jordan, with the most recent casualties reported in July.Hatami warns US over Gulf accessHatami used the announcement to reinforce Tehran's broader demand that Washington withdraw its forces from the region.His comments come as indirect communication between Iran and the US continues through mediators, although there has been no major diplomatic breakthrough following the collapse of the June peace framework.The two countries have instead remained locked in a tense standoff, with the Strait of Hormuz and waters around southern Iran emerging as key areas of confrontation.The bounty announcement further escalates the rhetoric between Tehran and Washington, even as both sides remain engaged through indirect channels aimed at preventing a wider conflict.
Article Summary: Iranian Army chief Amir Hatami offers $30,000 bounty for killing or capturing US soldiers. Reward doubled to $60,000 if the act is carried out by an Iranian woman. Announcement comes amid continued tensions between Tehran and Washington.

Article Title: Meet Jasper Gould and Emile Chilingirian: The two Brooklyn teenagers who built a Gen Z finance newsletter to nearly 60,000 subscribers while running a student investment group
Article Text:
​Representative Image of high school students running a youth-led financial media and investing operation (AI-generated image)

How Jasper Gould and Emile Chilingirian turned a shared interest in markets into a newsletter

Why the Brooklyn Youth Charitable Investment Group matters beyond the newsletter itself

What the newsletter's growth says about young people's interest in finance

Jasper Gould and Emile Chilingirian are juniors at the Berkeley Carroll School in Brooklyn, but much of their time outside class is spent on projects that look more like a small financial media company than a typical high school activity. The two founded the Brooklyn Youth Charitable Investment Group in September 2024, a student-run organisation designed to teach high schoolers about finance while giving them experience managing real investments and directing returns toward charitable causes. Alongside BYCIG, they created Passing the Torch, a finance and economics newsletter that has grown to around 57,000 subscribers, according to Gould, with readers that include professionals at major financial and technology companies. The publication describes itself as a youth-focused source of analysis covering markets, economics, politics and culture. What began as two teenagers exploring their interest in finance has since developed into a sizeable media operation with a readership extending well beyond their school community.According to the newsletter's own About page, Passing the Torch describes itself as a publication covering markets, economics, politics and culture, with an emphasis on research written for a younger audience.The publication's own pages currently give conflicting figures for how frequently it publishes: its About page says it produces 72 issues a year, while its homepage says it publishes more than 200 times a year and dozens of times a month. Because both figures appear on the newsletter's own website, the exact current publication frequency cannot be established from those pages alone. Gould has said he began learning about finance and investing independently as early as sixth grade, while Chilingirian joined him in developing the newsletter into a broader project aimed at connecting young people's perspectives with the financial world.The newsletter operates alongside the pair's other major project, the Brooklyn Youth Charitable Investment Group (BYCIG), a student-led organisation focused on financial education, investing and philanthropy. The group's public-facing pages currently contain conflicting information about its tax status: some describe BYCIG as a 501(c)(3) public charity, while other pages indicate that the organisation was still pursuing or expecting that status. The safest formulation is therefore to describe BYCIG as a student-led nonprofit initiative rather than state its tax-exempt status as an independently established fact.The organisation says it has grown to more than 1,000 members and that its investment portfolio increased by more than 25 per cent during its first year. Those figures are self-reported by the organisation and should not be presented as independently audited results. BYCIG says investment returns are directed toward charitable causes selected by its members, combining financial education with an investment and philanthropic component.The newsletter has also reported a readership approaching 60,000 subscribers, although this figure, like the membership and portfolio-growth statistics, is best attributed to the publication rather than presented as independently verified. Gould and Chilingirian have also developed other social-media projects around finance, extending their reach beyond the newsletter itself.Taken together, the projects show how two high-school students have built a surprisingly broad financial-media and education operation before entering university. But the most striking part may be the audience they are trying to reach: their newsletter explicitly positions itself as being built by youth and read by Wall Street, putting teenagers in the unusual position of producing financial commentary for both their peers and people already working in the industry.
Article Summary: Jasper Gould and Emile Chilingirian are juniors at the Berkeley Carroll School in Brooklyn. The two founded the Brooklyn Youth Charitable Investment Group in September 2024. The organisation is designed to teach high schoolers about finance while giving them experience managing real investments and directing returns toward charitable causes. Alongside BYCIG, they created Passing the Torch, a finance and economics newsletter that has grown to around 57,000 subscribers.

Article Title: Indian-origin CEO says he starts checking his emails at 4.30 am; 'If you want to work eight-to five...'
Article Text:
​Indian-origin CEO says work-life balance is not possible at the top.

Work-life balance not possible at the top, says CEO

Who is Khozema Shipchandler?

CEO Khozema Shipchandler said he starts checking his emails at 4.30 am that then wraps up his work at 9 pm. There is no day off and the Indian-origin CEO of Twilio runs laps around the house between meetings so that he does not spend all his time sitting as most of the time he's awake, he is working. In an interview with Fortune, he said that wanting work-life balance is awesome but sacrifice is what separates leaders from everyone else. For example, the 51-year-old CEO said he missed many of his son's tennis matches. The price that he paid made him a CFO when he was 31.On checking mails at 4.30 am, Shipchandler said he was always a morning person, and it helped him to remain ahead of others. Coffee, breakfast, browse through news headlines, and then a workout follow. “I do it in that order intentionally so that while I’m working out, I have an opportunity to think through the various things that have happened, through the course of the news, the things that I’ve seen on email and Slack and stuff like that," he said.Shipchandler is at work at 7.30 am which goes on till lunch. After lunch, he always immediately hits the treadmill for 10 minutes of walking so that he doesn’t get an afternoon lull.Then he takes a dinner break at 6.30 pm. Despite his traveling, he maintains the same routine. At 8 pm, he squeezes in another hour of extra work and then goes to sleep at 9.30 pm. On the weekend, he wakes up at 6.30 am and keeps his routine a little relaxed but he still works most Sundays.Shipchandler said he does not think that work-life balance is possible at the top but he insisted that he is not against smart working. “Every one of us has to make certain work-life choices,” he said. “This work-life choice obviously has certain consequences. I wasn’t there for all of my son’s tennis matches.”“If you want to work eight-to-five, coach your kids sports teams, have the evenings for yourself, and maybe another hobby or interest, that’s awesome,” Shipchandler said.He also doesn’t use social media and says that helps keep his focus.Shipchandler said he was built to work hard. “My parents were the classic immigrant success story, and as with many immigrant parents, they wanted their kids to do better than them and to create the opportunities for them,” he said. “They really pushed working hard and playing hard, which, by the way, I do play hard when I’m not working, so that was the goal,” he added.Shipchandler was born in Indiana to Indian parents who were from Mumbai. But his ancestral home is in Bengaluru. Khozema holds a Bachelor of Arts in Biology and English from Indiana University Bloomington. He started his career at GE and rose through the ranks to become the Chief Commercial Officer. After 22 years at GE, he joined Twilio and became the CEO in 2024.
Article Summary: Work-life balance not possible at the top, says Twilio CEO Khozema Shipchandler. The 51-year-old CEO said he missed many of his son's tennis matches. He started his career at GE and rose through the ranks to become the Chief Commercial Officer.

Article Title: In 1917, a South Dakota schoolteacher became America's first woman park ranger after being hired to guide visitors through a cave
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

How a South Dakota teacher helped open the door for women in America’s early park service

Wasson at an outcrop, circa 1920 (Image: Wikipedia)

Women were already entering the ranger service

The woman who changed the record books

A changing idea of what a park ranger could be

In the early years of America’s national parks, the ranger uniform was overwhelmingly associated with men. Women were already working in parks in various capacities, however, and some were beginning to take on duties that would later become central to the modern park ranger. One of the most remarkable early examples was a South Dakota schoolteacher who was hired in 1917 to guide visitors through Wind Cave in South Dakota. Her appointment reflected a period when the National Park Service and its predecessors were experimenting with how best to manage newly protected landscapes and explain them to growing numbers of visitors. The woman at the centre of this story was Isabel Bassett Wasson, who became one of the earliest women to hold a park ranger title in the United States. Her work at Yellowstone and her scientific background made her an important figure in the early history of women in the National Park Service. The story also reveals how the role of a ranger was changing from simply protecting park resources to educating visitors about the natural world.Wasson was born Isabel Deming Bassett in Brooklyn, New York, in January 1897. She studied at Wellesley College, where she earned a bachelor's degree, and later pursued a master's degree at Columbia University.She also taught at Wellesley College in 1918 and 1919. Her connection with national parks began through her interest in geology and natural history. In 1919, while visiting Yellowstone National Park as part of a tourist group, Wasson impressed park officials with her knowledge of the landscape and her ability to explain geological features to other visitors. Yellowstone superintendent Horace M. Albright was particularly impressed. According to the National Park Service, he described her as an excellent public speaker who could explain scientific subjects in language that ordinary visitors could understand. He subsequently offered her a position as a park ranger. Her appointment was significant because the ranger's role was still evolving. Wasson was not simply expected to perform clerical work. Albright specifically envisioned her guiding visitors around Yellowstone's geyser formations while helping protect those features. The Department of the Interior issued her a park ranger appointment in March 1920.Wasson's story is part of a much broader, and often overlooked, history of women working in America's national parks. The National Park Service notes that women served as rangers at Yellowstone during the 1920s, with several taking temporary appointments. Mary A. Rolfe, for example, worked as a ranger in 1921, while Frieda B. Nelson served during the 1925 season. Their responsibilities included interpreting the park for visitors, working in information offices and performing other duties associated with ranger work. Marguerite Lindsley also became a notable early figure. Born and raised at Yellowstone, she began working as a temporary ranger in 1921. In December 1925, she became the first woman appointed to a permanent ranger position at Yellowstone. For decades, she was widely described as the first permanent woman ranger in the entire National Park Service. But historical records later revealed that the story was more complicated.Research by the National Park Service eventually established that Mary J. Sullivan had actually received a permanent ranger appointment at Glacier National Park on July 1, 1924, 17 months before Lindsley's appointment at Yellowstone. Sullivan worked at the Polebridge entrance, where she registered visitors and vehicles. Her appointment appears to have been partly driven by practical considerations: she was married to Glacier ranger Thomas J. Sullivan and could live in existing ranger housing. Nevertheless, the NPS gave her an official permanent ranger appointment rather than a temporary position. The discovery changed the historical record. For nearly a century, Lindsley had been remembered as the first permanent woman park ranger, partly because newspaper coverage had made her story much more visible. Sullivan, by contrast, worked at a less prominent entrance, was older when appointed and spent only part of each year on duty. Her contribution consequently faded from public memory. The NPS's rediscovery of Sullivan's personnel records is a reminder that the history of America's national parks was not shaped only by the most famous rangers. Many women entered the service through modest, seasonal or overlooked positions, helping establish a path for women who would later take on increasingly diverse roles.The early women rangers also helped demonstrate that protecting a national park involved more than patrolling its boundaries. Their work connected science, education and conservation. Wasson's ability to explain geology to visitors was precisely what made her valuable to Yellowstone. Rather than keeping scientific knowledge within academic circles, she translated it into experiences that ordinary tourists could understand. Her work reflected the emerging idea that national parks should serve as places where the public could learn about America's landscapes as well as admire them. Although Wasson's own ranger appointment was relatively brief, her career became part of the foundation of women's participation in the National Park Service. The NPS's historical research now shows that women occupied ranger positions earlier and in greater numbers than older accounts suggested. The story also carries an important lesson about historical memory. The woman once remembered as the "first" was later joined, and partly displaced, by an earlier figure whose records had been overlooked. As the National Park Service's research demonstrates, recovering those forgotten records can change our understanding of who helped build America's national parks.
Article Summary: Isabel Bassett Wasson became one of the earliest women to hold a park ranger title in the United States. Her appointment reflected a period when the National Park Service and its predecessors were experimenting with how best to manage newly protected landscapes. Wasson's story is part of a much broader, and often overlooked, history of women working in America's national parks.

Article Title: Tupac Shakur murder trial begins after 3 decades, former gang leader Keffe D accused of killing rap icon
Article Text:
Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis pleads not guilty as Tupac Shakur murder trial opens in Las Vegas.

How Tupac was killed

Why Davis was charged years later

Gang rivalry at centre of case

The trial of Duane “Keffe D” Davis, the former street gang leader accused of orchestrating the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur, begins Monday in Las Vegas, nearly three decades after the hip-hop star was shot.Davis, 63, faces one count of murder with a deadly weapon in Clark County, Nevada, according to Reuters.He has pleaded not guilty.Prosecutors accuse Davis of organising the attack after a fight involving his nephew and Shakur's group at the MGM Grand casino on September 7, 1996.Shakur was travelling in a BMW with Marion “Suge” Knight, co-founder of Death Row Records, when a white Cadillac pulled alongside their vehicle near the Las Vegas Strip.Prosecutors allege Davis was in the Cadillac with three other men and had obtained the gun used in the shooting.Shakur was struck four times. He died in hospital six days later at the age of 25.Knight was also injured when a bullet fragment grazed his head.Investigators have never publicly established who fired the shots. The three other men who were in the Cadillac with Davis have since died.The investigation remained unresolved for decades before police focused again on Davis following statements he made publicly about the shooting.Authorities said Davis had discussed his role in interviews and in his 2019 memoir, “Compton Street Legend.”According to police, Davis said he was sitting in the front passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed the gun to one of the two men sitting behind him.Under Nevada law, prosecutors do not need to prove that Davis personally fired the weapon to secure a murder conviction. They must establish that he participated in the killing.The shooting followed a confrontation involving the South Side Compton Crips, which Davis has described himself as leading, and the Mob Piru group associated by police with Knight and Death Row Records.The groups were in Las Vegas for a heavyweight boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon when the fight at the MGM Grand took place.Authorities allege the shooting was carried out as retaliation for the earlier confrontation.The case became closely tied to the wider East Coast-West Coast rivalry that dominated hip-hop during the 1990s. Shakur's death intensified the violence and tension surrounding the rap scene at the time.Knight could potentially testify during the trial. He was with Shakur when the shooting happened and is currently serving a 28-year prison sentence for an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction.Shakur's killing remains one of the most closely watched unsolved crimes in music history. His death was followed six months later by the killing of fellow rapper Christopher Wallace, known as The Notorious B.I.G., in Los Angeles. That case remains unsolved.
Article Summary: Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, 63, faces one count of murder with a deadly weapon. He has pleaded not guilty to the 1996 killing of rapper Tupac Shakur. Shakur was shot four times and died in hospital six days later at the age of 25.

Article Title: A California school has been sued after a field trip of students who were encouraged to wear hijab, given Qurans
Article Text:
Zahra Billoo, CAIR official, called the lawsuit misguided and said the participation of the students in that field trip was voluntary.

School knew and did nothing, says lawsuit; School counters

Two Jewish parents, three former Jewish students, a Hindu parent and a Zoroastrian parent have sued Palo Alto Unified School District and Palo Alto High School principal Brent Kline after the students were encouraged to wear hijab and were given Qurans during what was supposed to be a field trip to a mosque. The incident took place last fall when the California school's Social Justice Pathway program conducted a field trip. The lawsuit said that the female students were encouraged to wear hijabs and the photos of the students were taken and posted online without taking the consent from the parents.The parents said the students were "exposed" to Zahra Billoo, the executive director of the Bay Area's office of the Council on American-Islamic Relations. The parents called Billoo controversial and alleged that she was given free access to students to advocate "personal religious and political views".The parents claimed that the school officials "knew or should have known of the recurring nature of the challenged field trips, the foreseeable risk that students would be exposed to religious activity and ideological messaging during those events, and the risk that student images would be captured and publicly disseminated in a religious context.”School superintendent Jason Glass issued a statement after the lawsuit and said they were yet to see the documents. “What I can say is what our board policy requires. Instruction about religion in our schools must be academic, not devotional. No faith may be promoted, and no faith may be denigrated,” Glass said. “Every family in this district is entitled to expect that standard, and I will review our practice against it. ”Billoo reacted to the lawsuit and called it'misguided'. “Public schools and the government have an obligation to remain neutral toward religion, but what neutrality does not mean is shielding students entirely,” Billoo said to San Francisco Chronicle. “The job of educators is to teach students, and expose them to different worldviews. That’s what happened here.”“One of the most important ways we combat hate is to learn about each other,” Billoo said, adding that the participation of the students was voluntary. “I am concerned that this group of parents not only wants to counteract that for their own children… but is attempting to intimidate schools and school districts from doing necessary work of educating the next generation.”
Article Summary: Jewish parents, three former Jewish students, a Hindu parent and a Zoroastrian parent have sued Palo Alto Unified School District and Palo Alto High School principal Brent Kline. The parents said the students were "exposed" to Zahra Billoo, the executive director of the Bay Area's office of the Council on American-Islamic Relations. Billoo said the participation of the students in that field trip was voluntary.

Article Title: Meet ex-Tesla engineer Saiman Shetty who became American citizen through EB-1 Green Card: 'That one decision gave me freedom'
Article Text:
Saiman Shetty, an ex-Tesla engineer, shared how he did not wait for H-1B and took the EB-1A path and now is a US citizen in 13 years.

What is Saiman Shetty's story?

'I built my profile from scratch'

What is EB1A Green Card?

When Saiman Shetty announced on social media that he lost his Green Card, several commentators celebrated without understanding the clickbait. In a video, ahead of the Indian Independence Day, he announced that the USCIS took away his Green Card. He said that a number of trolls reported him to the USCIS as he was helping other immigrants to get their Green Cards in the US. It was just a teaser to announce that USCIS took away his Green Card as he became a US citizen.Saiman Shetty runs Smart Immigration AI, which he calls the "first and oldest program helping high-skilled immigrants advance their career achievements into an extraordinary future in America". He is also the co-founder of ResumePuppy, a platform to make resumes for tech jobs.Before all these, he worked at Nuro, Lyft, Tesla and a few other companies in the US.But even before his US journey began, he did several internships in India, as his LinkedIn profile lists BSNL and ONGC as his workplaces.Shetty completed his engineering at Visvesvaraya Technological University in 2013 and then went to Arizona State University for his MS in electrical engineering.His US story spans from 2013 to 2026, during which he switched from a student visa to an Einstein visa and then straight to US citizenship.Recounting his US story, Shetty said that he was a broke international student with a one-way ticket, fighting it out in a new country -- first in his family to set foot in the US and he had no plan B."America did not roll out a red carpet. She beat me up. She tested me at every single turn. The debt I didn’t know how I’d repay. The jobs that said no. The H1B lottery I lost. The backlogs. Walking away from a comfortable Silicon Valley paycheck to go build something of my own. Every step, I had to prove myself. Again. And again," he wrote in his Instagram post."A few jealous pricks decided I was a “fraud” and built a neat little trap for me. Handed it to USCIS with a bow on top. And for a moment, the most powerful immigration system on earth almost took the bait," he said adding that he was investigated by the USCIS for his immigration platform and they finally adjudicated that he was not doing anything illegal.Shetty shared that after he did not get picked by the H-1B lottery, he built his profile from scratch and wrote his own petition for EB1A Green Card which is called the Einstein visa. "That one decision gave me freedom, stability, and a mission. I realized: no one should have to go through this alone," he said.The EB-1A visa (Employment-Based First Preference) is a US permanent residency option, commonly known as an "Einstein Green Card", designed for individuals who possess extraordinary ability in the sciences, arts, education, business, or athletics.You do not need an employer in the US to sponsor you and can file the petition for yourself. But there are certain conditions that one has to fulfil to become eligible for this Green Card.Winners of the Nobel Prize, Oscar, Grammy, or Olympians qualify for this Green Card straight away.The rest have to meet at least 3 of 10 criteria1. Lesser national or international prizes/awards for excellence.2. Membership in associations that require outstanding achievement.3. Published material about you or your work in major professional media.4. Participation as a judge or reviewer of the work of others in your field.5. Original scientific, scholarly, artistic, or business contributions of major significance.6. Authorship of scholarly articles in professional or major trade journals.7. Display of your work in artistic exhibitions or showcases.8. Performing a leading or critical role in distinguished organizations.9. Commanding a high salary or significantly high remuneration compared to peers.10. Commercial success in the performing arts (box office sales, stream counts).
Article Summary: Saiman Shetty, an ex-Tesla engineer, shared how he did not wait for H-1B and took the EB-1A path and now is a US citizen in 13 years. In a video, ahead of the Indian Independence Day, he announced that the USCIS took away his Green Card.

Article Title: US tourist killed by lightning strike while hiking on Italy’s Mount Etna
Article Text: A 29-year-old man from Kansas was killed by lightning while hiking on Mount Etna in Sicily, after being struck in an exposed area above the tree line, Italian firefighters said.The man was hit on Sunday evening and rescued from the volcano's slopes by helicopter. Medical personnel later declared him dead. His name has not been released.The incident occurred as Etna continues to experience prolonged volcanic activity. Authorities have closed large sections of the volcano's slopes to hikers because of the ongoing activity. However, it was not immediately clear whether the man was inside one of the restricted areas.The recent volcanic activity also disrupted flights at nearby Catania Airport, which was closed for much of the previous week because of ash emissions.Officials said lightning has caused more deaths on Mount Etna in recent decades than volcanic activity itself. The last fatalities directly linked to an eruption occurred in 1987.
